newsitem.title: UK: Nazi gold sale least of bullion market's worries.
newsitem.headline: Nazi gold sale least of bullion market's worries.

text.p: Even if all six tonnes of Nazi gold that still await return to original owners by the Tripartite Gold Commission (TGC) were sold tomorrow, the bullion market impact would be minimal, gold market analysts said on Tuesday.
The gold is all that remains of 377 tonnes recovered at the end of World War Two by allied forces after the rest was returned to national bank vaults ransacked during the war.

On Tuesday the TGC -- France, the UK and the United States -- announced it had frozen the return of 200,000 ounces (six tonnes) of looted gold to national bank vaults until it had established whether or not it belonged to Holocaust victims.
It has been suggested that the bullion should be used to establish a fund for the victims of the Nazi genocide.
According to the London Bullion Market Association, gold cleared through London daily in the last quarter of 1996 totalled 30 million ounces.
So "this is less than one percent," said bullion market analyst Tony Warwick-Ching at research group CRU International.
"A middle sized hedging operation (which happens regularly) by a gold miner would account for that," he added.
Rhona O'Connell, metal market analyst at stockbroker T. Hoare and Co said, "It is probably politically unacceptable to sell the gold and it is probably not 'good delivery' anyway.
"If they are going to freeze (distribution), they could lend it to the market at currently 2.5 percent per annum which would realise $1.87 million a year for a fund for holocaust victims," she added.

The gold market has been weakening since late last year pressured by rumours of sales of bullion from the vaults of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to aid poor countries and the European central banks.

As the price has fallen, gold miners anxious to lock in prices for the year to beat even lower prices, have added to the pressure by selling borrowed gold to be repaid by gold they will mine in the futures.
However, whether or not the TGC choses to sell eventually 200,000 ounces of gold is the least of the bullion market's current worries.
When the Dutch central bank announced in January it has sold 300 tonnes of gold late last year, anxiety over the national banks selling from their vaults was replaced with a hard-pressed stoicism.
Even that was overridden last week when rumours of another heavy sale sent the price falling to its lowest level in over three years.
"The overhead pressure (selling from gold miners) has finished," O'Connell said, adding that it could restart if interest rates and currency parities changed.
"What is a concern now, is the thought of interest rate cuts affecting the forward price the Australians get on their forward sales and a firmer Australian dollar reducing their income," she said.

O'Connell noted that the level of "shorts" in the market -- gold sold which is not yet owned on the basis that it can be bought and delivered in the future at a profitable price -- had fallen recently suggesting speculators were less convinced the price would weaken further.
"Speculators are less willing to go short than they were, but they not committed enough to buy-in," she said.
She added that the end of Ramadan in the Middle East and the beginning of the Indian Wedding Season shortly would bring physical demand for gold jewellery to one of its peaks of the year.
"The physical market in the Middle East has been very strong although it is probably exaggerated by shortage of material out of Australia," said CRU International's Warwick-Ching.
The market was likely to remain volatile and the search for a serious direction-finding factor would continue, Warwick-Ching suggested.
"We can expect some revelations over the next few weeks. There is still talk of a central bank sale and we had an (apparently) big sale last week," he said.

Both Warwick-Ching and O'Connell saw little on Monday's Eurostat ruling limiting the European central banks' use of gold sales revenue to reduce budget deficits to conform with EU criteria for monetary union.
"The capital gain gain cannot be used for deficit reduction but the interest earned can be. There is still an incentive for the banks to sell," Warwick-Ching said.

O'Connell reasoned that prudence would limit central bank sales ambitions. "If the federation of Europe founders (and currency market turmoil ensues), the citizenry will not be happy if they find their central bank has given all their gold away," she said.
